misconceptions.description: Believing that constant speed implies zero acceleration on a curved path
misconceptions.trigger: learner reports zero acceleration for circular motion at constant speed
misconceptions.feedback: Speed is the magnitude of velocity. Direction is also part of velocity. Constant speed on a curve means a_t = 0 but a_n = v²/ρ ≠ 0.

misconceptions.description: Believing the choice of coordinate system does not matter for problem tractability
misconceptions.trigger: learner uses Cartesian for satellite tracking or polar for a bead on a wire
misconceptions.feedback: Pick coordinates to match the geometry. n-t for path-defined motion; polar for origin-anchored motion. Wrong choice multiplies algebraic effort and error rate.

misconceptions.description: Computing polar acceleration as just (r̈, θ̈) without the rotating-basis cross terms
misconceptions.trigger: learner writes a_r = r̈ and a_θ = θ̈ in a polar problem
misconceptions.feedback: Polar basis vectors rotate. The full decomposition is a_r = r̈ - rθ̇² and a_θ = rθ̈ + 2ṙθ̇. The cross terms are not optional.

misconceptions.description: Drawing the normal unit vector û_n away from the center of curvature instead of toward it
misconceptions.trigger: learner sets û_n outward on a curved path
misconceptions.feedback: û_n always points toward the center of curvature (inside of the turn). Outward direction flips the sign of the centripetal force equation.
